newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA ROVIC ENDS BODY HUNT, MULLS NEW MINE.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA ROVIC ENDS BODY HUNT, MULLS NEW MINE.

text.p: The programme to recover the bodies of 16 men killed in a mudslide at South Africa's Roberts Victor Diamond Mine (Rovic), had been suspended, the mine's owners said on Wednesday.

Vancouver-listed Botswana Diamondfields Inc said underground conditions had become too hazardous despite careful steps to prevent any further mud or water inflow into the workings, and on December 24 a second inflow had occurred.
In November last year an inflow of mud from old open cast workings into the underground shafts killed 19 miners and a contract driller. Four bodies were subsequently recovered.
Norman Lock, a director of Botswana Diamondfields, said on Wednesday the feasibility of a completely new mine layout with new shafts going to greater depths was being investigated.

Fears of further mud inflows at the mine, which is based at Dealesville, 60 kilometres from the Free State capital of Bloemfontein, will limit the current mine's sub-surface workings to the pumping of water.
In a bid to mitigate the production standstill, coarse plant tailings would be recrushed and Rovic was considering re-treating old tailings which were known to contain diamonds.
Miners would be offered work on other properties but a number may have to be retrenched until a decision is made whether to continue with the new mine, the owners said.

Lock said substantial diamondiferous kimberlite reserves exist below the present mining levels. He hoped these could be reached with new layouts which would operate at higher tonnages and lower operating costs.
New plans would allow for the mining of as much as 5-million tonnes of kimberlite over the mine's life, he said.
An official enquiry into the mud disaster will be held on January 27.
